items.stem: Actual economic growth is
options: an increase in the productive capacity of the economy
an increase in nominal GDP only
an increase in the price level
items.answer: an increase in real GDP
items.markingKey: Measured by % change in real GDP; shown by a movement towards/along the PPC or a rightward AD shift with spare capacity.

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, explain the difference between actual and potential growth.
items.answer: PPC diagram: actual growth is a movement from a point inside the PPC towards it (using unemployed resources); potential growth is an outward shift of the PPC (more or better resources). In AD/AS: actual = rise in real output, potential = rightward shift of LRAS.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: actual growth; 1 mark: potential growth; 1 mark: diagram description [3]

items.stem: Explain why a negative output gap may cause inflation to fall.
items.answer: With spare capacity and unemployment, firms face weak demand and workers have little bargaining power, so firms hold down prices and wage growth slows.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: spare capacity; 1 mark: weak price and wage pressure [2]

items.stem: Potential GDP in Merania is $1200 billion and actual GDP is $1164 billion. Calculate the output gap as a percentage of potential GDP.

Real GDP growth in Westaria over five years was 3%, 3.5%, 1%, -0.5%, 2.5%. Potential output grew at a steady 2% a year, and the output gap was zero at the start. Calculate the index of real GDP (start = 100) and the output gap at the end of each year, and identify the phases of the business cycle.
items.answer: Real GDP index: 103, 106.6, 107.7, 107.1, 109.8; output gap: 1%, 2.5%, 1.5%, -1%, -0.5%. Boom where growth exceeds trend and the gap is positive; downturn/recession when growth is negative; recovery afterwards.
items.markingKey: Index compounding [2]; potential index and gap = (actual − potential)/potential [2]; phases identified with reference to growth vs trend [2].

items.stem: Extract: Dravonia has grown at 8% a year for a decade, driven by manufacturing exports and coal-fired power. Carbon emissions have risen by 5% a year and air pollution in Kuala Lumpur is severe. The government plans to raise growth further through infrastructure spending. (a) Explain whether emissions growth shows decoupling. (b) Explain one policy to make the growth more sustainable.
items.answer: (a) Relative decoupling: emissions grow more slowly than GDP. (b) Carbon tax/permits, subsidies for renewables, regulation of emissions, investment in public transport.

items.stem: Potential economic growth is
options: an increase in the productive capacity of the economy
an increase in real GDP from spare capacity
items.answer: an increase in the productive capacity of the economy
items.markingKey: Outward shift of the PPC or LRAS.

items.stem: Explain two causes of fluctuations in the business cycle.
items.answer: Changes in investment (accelerator), consumer confidence, external shocks (commodity prices, world demand), financial crises, government policy changes, multiplier–accelerator interaction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain two causes of fluctuations in the business cycle. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain the difference between actual and potential growth.
items.answer: (a) Changes in investment (accelerator), consumer confidence, external shocks (commodity prices, world demand), financial crises, government policy changes, multiplier–accelerator interaction. (b) PPC diagram: actual growth is a movement from a point inside the PPC towards it (using unemployed resources); potential growth is an outward shift of the PPC (more or better resources). In AD/AS: actual = rise in real output, potential = rightward shift of LRAS.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4] (b) 1 mark: actual growth; 1 mark: potential growth; 1 mark: diagram description [3]

items.stem: Potential GDP in Valdoria is $500 billion and actual GDP is $507.5 billion. Calculate the output gap as a percentage of potential GDP.

Real GDP growth in Dravonia over five years was 2.5%, 4%, 1.5%, -0.5%, 2%. Potential output grew at a steady 2% a year, and the output gap was zero at the start. Calculate the index of real GDP (start = 100) and the output gap at the end of each year, and identify the phases of the business cycle.
items.answer: Real GDP index: 102.5, 106.6, 108.2, 107.7, 109.8; output gap: 0.5%, 2.5%, 2%, -0.5%, -0.5%. Boom where growth exceeds trend and the gap is positive; downturn/recession when growth is negative; recovery afterwards.
items.markingKey: Index compounding [2]; potential index and gap = (actual − potential)/potential [2]; phases identified with reference to growth vs trend [2].

items.stem: Umbria Nova has experienced three recessions in fifteen years. (a) Explain the phases of the business cycle and the meaning of an output gap. (b) ‘Governments should try to eliminate the business cycle.’ Discuss this view.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Fluctuations cause unemployment, uncertainty and inflation. (b) Case for the view: Fluctuations cause unemployment, uncertainty and inflation. Case against / evaluation: Some fluctuation is unavoidable and reallocates resources; policy lags and forecasting errors may worsen cycles; stabilisation rather than elimination. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Which policy is most likely to increase potential growth?
options: Increased spending on education and training
A rise in the interest rate
items.answer: Increased spending on education and training
items.markingKey: Raises the quality of labour, shifting LRAS right.

items.stem: Explain how supply-side policies can promote sustained economic growth.
items.answer: Education, training, R&D incentives, infrastructure and competition policy raise productivity and the quantity/quality of factors, shifting LRAS right so output can grow without inflation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: policy; 1 mark: productivity/capacity; 1 mark: LRAS shift, non-inflationary [3]

items.stem: Explain why demand-side policies alone cannot sustain economic growth in the long run.
items.answer: Once the output gap is closed, extra AD raises prices rather than output; long-run growth requires more capacity (LRAS shifts).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: capacity constraint; 1 mark: inflation rather than growth [2]

items.stem: Real GDP per head in Marvona grows at 3.5% a year. Using the rule of 70, calculate how long it takes to double.
items.answer: 20 years

items.stem: GDP per head in Tarvia is $2,000 and grows at 8% a year; in Esteria it is $20,000 and grows at 1% a year. Calculate GDP per head in each country after 10 years and the ratio of Esteria’s to Tarvia’s income now and then. Explain one policy that might have allowed Tarvia to grow so fast.
items.answer: Tarvia: $4318; Esteria: $22,092. Ratio falls from 10 to 5.1. Policy: high investment in infrastructure and education, openness to FDI and trade, which raise productivity (catch-up growth).
items.markingKey: Compound growth Y × (1 + g)ⁿ for each [2]; ratios [1]; policy linked to productivity/capacity [2].

items.stem: Extract: Zentara has grown at 6% a year for a decade, driven by manufacturing exports and coal-fired power. items.answer: (a) No decoupling: emissions grow at least as fast as GDP. (b) Carbon tax/permits, subsidies for renewables, regulation of emissions, investment in public transport.

items.stem: According to the “rule of 70”, an economy growing at 3.5% a year doubles its real GDP in about
items.answer: 20 years

items.answer: Higher post-tax returns encourage investment, raising AD in the short run and the capital stock (and productivity) in the long run, shifting LRAS right.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: investment incentive; 1 mark: AD and LRAS effects [2]

items.stem: The government of Valdoria wants to raise its trend growth rate from 1.5% to 3%. ‘Supply-side policies are the most effective way to achieve long-run economic growth.’ Discuss this view.
items.answer: Arguments for: Supply-side raises productive capacity non-inflationarily. Arguments against / evaluation: Long time lags, costly, uncertain effects; demand-side needed in recessions; policy mix best. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Sustainable economic growth is growth that
options: is faster than the world average
meets the needs of the present without reducing the ability of future generations to meet their needs

items.markingKey: Brundtland definition.

items.stem: Explain why economic growth may not be sustainable.
items.answer: It may rely on depleting non-renewable resources and creating pollution and climate change whose costs fall on future generations; GDP ignores this loss of natural capital.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: resource depletion/pollution; 1 mark: future costs; 1 mark: GDP ignores [3]

items.stem: Explain how growth can provide the resources to improve the environment.
items.answer: Higher incomes give tax revenue for environmental protection, fund cleaner technology, and consumers demand cleaner goods (environmental Kuznets curve).

items.stem: In Merania, real GDP rose from $600 billion to $636 billion in a year, while carbon emissions changed from 250 million tonnes to 257.5 million tonnes. Calculate the emissions intensity of GDP (tonnes per $1,000 of GDP) in each year and the percentage change, and explain whether growth has been decoupled from emissions.
items.answer: Intensity: 416.67 and 404.87 tonnes per $1,000; change -2.8%. Relative decoupling: emissions grew more slowly than GDP.
items.markingKey: Intensity = emissions/GDP each year [2]; % change [1]; correct classification of decoupling [1].

items.stem: Quentara is one of the fastest-growing economies in its region but also one of the most polluted. (a) Explain the costs and benefits of economic growth. (b) Discuss whether the environmental costs of economic growth outweigh its benefits.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Pollution, resource depletion, climate change, inequality. (b) Case for the view: Pollution, resource depletion, climate change, inequality. Case against / evaluation: Higher living standards, poverty reduction, resources for environmental protection; green technology and decoupling; depends on country. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.
